tweets.title: With LLMs increasingly used in software development, the bottleneck will move from writing code to reasoning about code (review, testing, debugging, and verific
tweets.body: With LLMs increasingly used in software development, the bottleneck will move from writing code to reasoning about code (review, testing, debugging, and verification). Dynamically typed languages like Python are popular because they made code easy to write. However, the future will belong to languages that make code easy to reason about, and Lean holds substantial promise in that regard @leanprover. Very excited about our new work on verifiable code generation led by @0xlf_ !

tweets.body: Surprised to see the Gemma 3 Technical Report (https://t.co/I1rKry8rnc) using our SpatialSense benchmark to evaluate multimodal performance. Ah, the good old days.

tweets.title: Here are 18 proofs generated by o3-mini (https://t.co/a8QYLPK05V) and R1 (https://t.co/7DLMugyI9p). For each failed proof, we annotated the first error—most of
tweets.body: Here are 18 proofs generated by o3-mini (https://t.co/a8QYLPK05V) and R1 (https://t.co/7DLMugyI9p). For each failed proof, we annotated the first error—most of which are easy to spot once pointed out. However, detecting these errors in long proofs is extremely challenging for humans, even though the domain only requires high-school math. Verifying advanced mathematical proofs manually would be even harder, reinforcing the need for formal mathematical reasoning with proof assistants like Lean @leanprover . Read our position paper for more details: https://t.co/0rsmiGZLgw.

tweets.title: Clarification: I missed an important qualifier in Yong's original post: Goedel-Prover outperforms all existing open-source methods on PutnamBench, but it perfor
tweets.body: Clarification: I missed an important qualifier in Yong's original post: Goedel-Prover outperforms all existing open-source methods on PutnamBench, but it performs on par with ABEL (both proved 7 theorems). It’s ranked #1 on the PutnamBench Leaderboard due to slightly lower compute usage (Pass@512 vs. Pass@596). However, this gap is minor and could be influenced by factors like hardware or implementation details.

tweets.body: While constructing LeanEuclid, we discovered some fascinating ambiguities in Euclid's work. For example, below is Proposition 24 in Elements. Euclid’s proof assumes the triangles resemble the diagram on the left. But what if they looked like the ones on the right? Is his original proof still valid? (Hint: Find the answer in Appendix B of our paper!)
